subject: Cooking
title: You Don't Need to Wash Chicken Before Cooking
description: A 60-second lesson on You Don't Need to Wash Chicken Before Cooking.

hook.text: Washing raw chicken before cooking is a tradition in many households. Health agencies say: stop doing it.

buildup.text: Running water over chicken doesn't remove bacteria. Salmonella and Campylobacter cling to the surface.

discovery.text: Washing splashes contaminated water droplets up to 3 feet around the sink — onto counters, dishes, and hands.

twist.text: Cooking chicken to 165°F kills all dangerous bacteria. Water at any temperature cannot.

climax.text: The USDA, FDA, and NHS all explicitly advise against washing poultry — yet 70% of home cooks still do it.

punchline.text: Washing chicken doesn't clean it. It spreads the problem.

quiz.question: Why do health agencies advise against washing raw chicken?
options: Splashing spreads bacteria to surrounding surfaces

details.summary: Washing raw chicken does not remove bacteria — it spreads them around your kitchen through water splashes. Salmonella and Campylobacter survive rinsing but are completely killed by proper cooking to 165°F. Health authorities worldwide advise against washing poultry before cooking.
details.whyItMatters: This counterintuitive tip could prevent foodborne illness. Washing raw chicken is one of the most common kitchen practices that actually increases contamination risk rather than reducing it.
takeaways: Water splashes can spread bacteria up to 3 feet from the sink
Cooking to 165°F kills all harmful chicken bacteria completely
USDA, FDA, and WHO all advise against washing raw poultry

faq.question: How far can bacteria splash when washing chicken?
faq.answer: USDA research showed that water droplets carrying bacteria can splash onto surrounding surfaces, utensils, and ready-to-eat foods up to 3 feet away. These invisible splashes are nearly impossible to track and clean, creating contamination you cannot see.

faq.question: What should you do after handling raw chicken?
faq.answer: Cook the chicken to 165°F internal temperature — this kills all pathogens. Wash hands with soap for 20 seconds after handling. Sanitize any surfaces and utensils that contacted raw chicken. Use separate cutting boards for raw poultry to prevent cross-contamination.
